## The idea

Pitch tells you which note is sounding, and an oscillator supplies raw colour, but neither fully describes the gesture. A note that reaches full level at once behaves differently from one that swells slowly into view. A long fading tail occupies musical space differently from an abrupt stop. Much of what a listener recognises as instrumental character lies in this change of amplitude over time.

An *envelope* divides that change into attack, decay, sustain, and release. Attack is the rise toward a peak. Decay moves from that peak toward a held sustain level. Sustain describes the maintained portion, and release is the return to silence after the held portion ends. Sonic Pi exposes these segments as parameters, which makes an envelope readable as data.

The program fixes the `:prophet` synth and C4, then plays four envelope hashes. Hear them as four gestures made from the same pitch and oscillator: a clipped sound, a swell, a held note, and a note with a lingering release.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 60
use_synth :prophet

envelopes = [
  {attack: 0.0, decay: 0.05, sustain: 0.1, release: 0.1},
  {attack: 1.2, decay: 0.2, sustain: 0.6, release: 0.4},
  {attack: 0.01, decay: 0.5, sustain: 1.2, release: 0.3},
  {attack: 0.02, decay: 0.2, sustain: 0.4, release: 2.0}
]

envelopes.each do |shape|
  play :c4, **shape, amp: 0.8
  sleep 3
end
```

The first envelope schedules a very short event, while the second takes more than a beat to reach its peak. The third begins sharply and maintains a longer body; because the hash does not lower `sustain_level`, its decay value does not create the pronounced drop that a lower plateau would. The fourth totals about 2.62 beats before any synth-specific tail, so it occupies most of the three-beat slot without necessarily crossing into the next one. Audition the four gestures before attaching stronger perceptual descriptions.

## Change one thing

1. Set the slow envelope's attack to `2`. The note now spends most of its slot approaching the peak. Listen for the difference between knowing when the code triggered and hearing when the note seems to arrive.

2. Restore the original and raise the percussive envelope's release from `0.1` to `1.5`. Its attack remains sharp, but the tail fills what was previously silence. This changes connection without moving an onset.

3. Restore the envelopes and add `sustain_level: 0.2` to the held shape. Attend to the decay from the initial peak. A lower plateau makes that internal drop easier to hear.

Keep pitch, synth, and the other envelope segments fixed during each edit. Attack, release, and sustain level then reveal three different parts of the note's history.

## Why it works

An envelope behaves like a state machine over amplitude. It moves from silence to peak, from peak to a sustained level, and from that level back to silence. The segments are related phases of one gesture, not four independent effects. Changing the attack alters how the listener locates the beginning; changing the release alters how the note gives up its space.

Scheduling and envelope time remain separate. `sleep 3` determines when the next event is triggered. It does not force the current sound to end at that boundary. A release longer than the sleep can overlap the next note, while a short envelope may leave silence before the next trigger. This difference will become important when rhythm examples distinguish an absent attack from a tail still fading through a rest.

The four hashes make the shapes inspectable. You can compare their attack values, sort them by release, or copy one profile to another pitch without rendering anything. Playback supplies the missing perceptual information: synth implementations have their own response curves, and extreme settings may not sound proportional to their numbers. Compare envelope shapes on one synth before assuming another synth will behave identically.

Later terms such as staccato, legato, and accent will draw on these same variables. A detached note usually combines a clear attack with a short sounding body. A connected line may overlap releases across successive onsets. An accent can involve amplitude, attack, or both. The vocabulary becomes more useful once you can hear which segment carries the effect.

Part 2 will set timbre aside and organise pitches into a twelve-class cycle. The envelope does not disappear; it returns whenever those pitches need clearer separation or a different kind of connection.

## Take it further

Choose a short recorded sound available on your computer and listen to its amplitude shape rather than its pitch. Decide whether the attack is immediate or gradual, whether the level falls after the peak, whether a body remains, and how the sound returns to silence. Encode that estimate as a fifth envelope hash and alternate it with the four references.

The aim is a recognisable gesture, not an exact imitation of the recording's timbre. Record which envelope segment controls each audible difference and note any feature the four-stage model cannot express. Audition the result in Sonic Pi 5, because valid Ruby can establish the shape of the data but cannot reveal the synth's actual response curve.
